title: A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence applications are being used to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in higher education, and what benefits, drawbacks, theories, and implementation patterns appear in the empirical literature. The review is motivated by growing use of AI in higher education alongside a recognized need to connect these tools to established learning theory, especially SRL frameworks.

Using a qualitative systematic review guided by PRISMA, the authors identified 14 empirical studies on AI-supported SRL in higher education. The reviewed interventions included chatbots, explainable AI dashboards and evaluation systems, automated writing evaluation tools, serious games with intelligent tutoring features, and an AI-enriched e-textbook. Across studies, these tools were used to support different SRL phases such as goal setting, progress monitoring, help-seeking, feedback, and self-evaluation.

The evidence base covered university students in higher education contexts, with most studies involving STEM or language-learning tasks and a smaller number addressing non-academic areas such as communication skills and exam anxiety. The studies were geographically diverse, including work from China, Sweden, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Ukraine, Australia, Spain, Finland, and New Zealand. Because this is a review, no single implementation setting or duration applies consistently across all included studies.

The main conclusion is that AI shows promise for supporting SRL, especially in the performance phase through real-time guidance, monitoring, feedback, and help-seeking support. However, support is often partial rather than holistic across all SRL phases, and outcomes are mixed depending on tool design, learner characteristics, and the balance between human-centered and AI-centered regulation. The review also highlights concerns about usability, feedback accuracy, inconsistent gains in self-efficacy, and the need for stronger theory-building and more rigorous empirical research on AI-supported SRL.

finding.finding_summary: In the review's summary of Nguyen et al., students who engaged in iterative, highly interactive processes with a generative AI assisting tool such as ChatGPT tended to achieve better writing performance than those using AI only as a supplementary source in a linear process.

In the review's summary of Kuzminska et al., use of AI tools mainly focused on ChatGPT and Notion AI did not improve social engagement or self-efficacy dynamics overall, though there was a positive effect for students with average self-efficacy.
